before.content_html:
Making, Quality and Evaluation

Once a design has been fully developed, the final stage of the non-exam assessment moves from planning to production. This lesson covers how a prototype is manufactured safely and accurately, how its quality is checked against the specification, and how it is tested and evaluated once complete — including assessing its environmental impact. These are the skills examiners reward most highly across the whole project, so it is worth understanding exactly what each stage demands.

Manufacturing the Prototype

Manufacturing a high-quality prototype means selecting the right materials, tools and techniques for the job. This includes hand tools, machinery and digital manufacture, alongside fixtures, templates, patterns and a jig where components need to be repeated accurately. Every choice should be justified — a student who explains why a material or tool was chosen shows more understanding than one who simply lists what was used, and this justification is exactly what examiners are looking for.

Accuracy also depends on working within tolerance and cutting materials efficiently to minimise waste. A prototype that is 3 mm out on a joint might still fit, but one that is 3 cm out will not — checking measurements regularly during manufacture, not just at the end, prevents small errors becoming large ones that cannot be corrected later.

Key Fact

Safe working practice must be demonstrated for both the maker and others throughout manufacture — for example wearing appropriate protective equipment, using guards on machinery and keeping a tidy, hazard-free workspace.

Quality and Accuracy

Once the prototype is complete, its quality must be checked. This means measuring the degree to which it performs as intended and confirming it is accurately assembled and finished. Quality control should happen throughout manufacture, not only at the end, so problems can be corrected before more time and material is wasted.

A student making a set of four identical box lids checks each one against the working drawing after cutting, tests that every lid fits its box before assembly, and inspects the applied finish for an even colour with no brush marks. Any lid that fails a check is reworked or remade before moving on, rather than being left until the end.

Key Fact

Accuracy is how closely a prototype matches its working drawing and specification; quality also includes the standard of finish, assembly and how well it performs its intended function.

Testing Under Realistic Conditions

A finished prototype must be tested under realistic conditions to check it is fit for purpose. This means using the product as the intended user would, not just checking it looks correct. Results should be recorded and compared against the product specification written earlier in the project.

A student designs a phone stand for use at a bedside. To test it under realistic conditions, they place a phone on the stand at different angles, check it does not tip when the screen is tapped, and leave it in position overnight to see whether it holds its shape. Each result is compared against the specification point it was meant to satisfy.

Evaluating Against the Specification

Evaluation means analysing the results of testing and judging whether the prototype meets each point of the product specification. A strong evaluation does not just describe what happened — it weighs up strengths and weaknesses, considers what could be changed, and reaches a conclusion about how successful the prototype is overall.

Sustainability is evaluated using a life cycle assessment (LCA). This considers the impact of extracting raw materials, manufacturing and transporting the product, its use by the consumer, and what happens to it once it is thrown away or recycled.

Key Fact

A life cycle assessment covers four key stages: raw material extraction, manufacture and transportation, use by the consumer, and final disposal or recycling.

Choosing the Right Command Word

Make and evaluate questions often use different command words that require different responses. “Describe” asks for the main steps or features of something. “Discuss” asks students to identify the issue in the question, explore all aspects of it with reasoning, and come to a conclusion. “Evaluate” goes further — it needs a substantiated judgement built from weighing up strengths, weaknesses and alternatives, supported by evidence. Treating these command words as interchangeable is one of the most common reasons marks are lost.

“Calculate” questions also need care. Marks are awarded for the correct method as well as the final answer, so workings should always be shown. For example, if a batch of components needs 250 mm strips of timber cut from 2400 mm stock lengths costing £3.20 each, the method is \(\text{stock length} \div \text{piece length}\) to find pieces per length, then \(\text{components needed} \div \text{pieces per length}\), rounded up, to find the number of stock lengths, before multiplying by the price per length.

Communicating Design Ideas

Coming up with a good idea is only half the job. A designer must show that idea to other people — clients, users, manufacturers — clearly enough that they understand it without confusion. Section 1.17 of the specification lists techniques for developing, communicating, recording and justifying design ideas. In your non-exam assessment, section 2.4 asks you to use a range of these techniques to present your ideas effectively.

Freehand Sketching & Annotation

At the start of a project, ideas need to be captured quickly before they are lost. Freehand sketching lets a designer explore many possibilities in a short time, without worrying about neatness or scale. Annotated sketches add written notes to a sketch — pointing out materials, dimensions, colours, or how a mechanism works. Annotation turns a rough drawing into something another person can actually understand and act on.

Key Fact

A freehand sketch shows shape and form quickly, but annotation is what communicates function, materials and dimensions to someone who was not there when the idea was drawn.

3D Views: Isometric, Oblique and Perspective Drawing

Once an idea needs to look more realistic, designers move to 3D drawing systems. Isometric drawing keeps every measurement to scale, which makes it useful for showing accurate proportions. Oblique drawing is quicker to construct because the front face is drawn exactly as it would be seen in 2D, with only the depth lines angled back.

Perspective drawing is the most realistic of the three because it uses vanishing points, making distant parts of the object appear smaller. This makes it good for client presentations, but it is harder to draw accurately and is not to scale, so it is rarely used for manufacturing detail.

Use isometric drawing when accurate proportions matter, such as showing a client how big a product will actually be. Use oblique drawing when speed matters more than full realism — it is often used for quick concept views with a curved or detailed front face, since that face stays undistorted. Use perspective drawing when the priority is showing how a product will look and feel in a real setting, such as a chair in a living room, even though it sacrifices scale accuracy.

Orthographic Projection, Exploded Views & Assembly Drawings

When a design is ready to be made, it needs a formal technical drawing that a manufacturer can work from without asking the designer questions. Orthographic projection shows the front, side and plan views of a product, each drawn accurately to scale using conventions such as dimension lines, centre lines and dashed lines for hidden detail. Because every measurement is exact, this is the standard format for working drawings.

Some products are made of several parts that need to be shown fitting together. An exploded view pulls the components apart along a line so the order of assembly is clear. An assembly drawing does the opposite — it shows the parts already joined, so a maker can check how the finished product should look before fixing anything permanently.

Key Fact

An exploded view separates parts to show assembly order; an assembly drawing shows the same parts already joined together in their finished position.

Schematic Diagrams, CAD and Written Techniques

Not every design idea is about physical shape. A schematic diagram shows how the parts of a system — such as an electronic circuit — are logically connected, using standard symbols rather than realistic drawings. This is especially useful for the Systems material category, where a designer needs to show inputs, processes and outputs clearly.

Computer-aided design (CAD) lets a designer build an accurate digital model, rotate it to check every angle, apply realistic colours and materials, and even run simple simulations before anything is physically made. CAD files can also be sent straight to computer-aided manufacture (CAM) equipment such as a laser cutter, which speeds up the move from idea to prototype and reduces wasted material from mistakes made on paper.

Drawings alone rarely tell the whole story. Written techniques record and justify decisions — explaining, for example, why a particular material was chosen or how a feature meets a user’s need. Examiners marking NEA portfolios specifically look for design ideas that are communicated and justified using written explanation as well as visual techniques.

Choosing the Right Technique for the NEA

Section 2.4 of the NEA rewards a considered selection of techniques, not simply a large number of them. A strong portfolio might move from quick annotated freehand sketches during initial ideas, through an isometric or CAD-rendered view to show the chosen design clearly, to a third-angle orthographic drawing with full dimensions ready for manufacture. Matching the technique to its purpose — quick exploration, client communication, or manufacturing instruction — shows genuine understanding, not just drawing practice.

Physical and Working Properties in Depth

The core content introduces the main materials in each category, but the specialist section pushes further. This lesson looks at extra metals, papers, polymers, systems components, textiles and timbers you need for your chosen material category, and the physical and working properties that let you compare any material scientifically.

Advanced Metals: High Carbon Steel, Tungsten Steel & Titanium

High carbon steel contains more carbon than mild steel. This makes it very hard and able to hold a sharp edge, but also brittle, so it is used for cutting tools, chisels and blades rather than structural parts that might bend. Tungsten steel is an alloy of steel and tungsten. It keeps its hardness even at high temperatures caused by friction, which is why it is used for high-speed cutting tools and drill bits.

Titanium is light, strong and highly resistant to corrosion. These properties make it ideal for aerospace parts and medical implants such as hip replacements, where the metal must not react with the human body. Its main disadvantages are cost and the difficulty of machining it, since it work-hardens quickly and generates a lot of heat when cut.

Key Fact

High carbon steel is hard but brittle; tungsten steel stays hard at high temperatures; titanium is light, strong and corrosion-resistant but expensive to machine.

Papers, Boards and Packaging Laminates

Beyond copier paper, cartridge paper, tracing paper, folding boxboard, corrugated board and solid white board, the specification also covers foil-lined board and packaging laminate, the material used for cartons like Tetra Pak. Combining several materials in one laminate gives packaging properties that no single material could offer on its own.

Physical characteristics used to describe paper and board include density (how heavy the material feels for its size), transparency and surface texture. These characteristics affect how well a material prints, folds or bonds to other layers without cracking.

A carton of long-life milk needs to be rigid, leak-proof and keep out light and oxygen so the contents do not spoil without refrigeration. Paperboard gives the structure and a printable surface for branding. A thin layer of polyethylene bonds the layers together and seals against liquid. A layer of aluminium foil blocks light and oxygen. Together, the laminate does a job that paperboard alone could never do.

Additional Thermoforming Polymers: ABS, PET & PVC

Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) is tough and resistant to impact, which is why it is used for products that get knocked around, such as construction bricks and power tool casings. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is lightweight, transparent and can be blow moulded into thin-walled shapes, making it the standard choice for drinks bottles because it also resists gases escaping or entering.

Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) can be manufactured as a rigid or a flexible polymer depending on the additives used, so the same base material is used for both drainage pipes and flexible cable insulation. When comparing polymers for an exam answer, always link the property, such as tensile strength or impact resistance, to the actual use of the product.

Key Fact

ABS resists impact and suits casings; PET is blow moulded into drinks bottles; PVC is made rigid for pipes or flexible for cable insulation.

Systems: Microcontrollers and PIC Chips

A microcontroller, often called a PIC, is a control device that gives a product its programmable behaviour. Instead of wiring separate switches and logic gates for every function, a single microcontroller can be programmed with a flowchart-based routine that reads inputs, makes decisions, and switches outputs on or off, including delays, loops and counts.

Additional Textiles: Regenerated Cellulosic Fibres

Viscose, acetate and Tencel are examples of regenerated cellulosic fibre. They start life as wood pulp or cotton linters, which are dissolved and pushed through tiny holes to form new fibres. This gives them a soft handle and good drape like a natural fibre, while offering some of the consistency of a synthetic fibre, which is why they are often used for linings and lightweight clothing.

Natural fibres like wool and cotton absorb moisture well but can lose strength when wet. Synthetic fibres like polyester and nylon keep their strength when wet and resist creasing, but do not breathe as well. Regenerated fibres like viscose sit in between, offering comfort closer to natural fibres but with some of the manufacturing consistency of a synthetic. Choosing between them means weighing elasticity, breathability and durability against the end use of the product.

Additional Timbers: Jelutong, Larch & Chipboard

Jelutong is a pale, straight-grained hardwood that is very easy to carve and shape, so it is often chosen for pattern-making and modelling rather than finished furniture. Larch is a durable softwood that resists rot even outdoors, making it a common choice for cladding and fencing. Chipboard is a manufactured board made from wood chips bonded together with resin under heat and pressure. It is cheap and available in large flat sheets, which is why it is widely used as the core material in flat-pack furniture.

Physical & Working Properties: The Common Language

Whichever material category you study, examiners expect you to compare materials using the same properties. Density tells you how heavy a material feels for its size — useful when comparing a lightweight polymer casing to a heavier metal one.

Conductivity explains why metals are chosen for wiring and heat sinks, while polymers and timbers are chosen as insulators to keep people safe from heat or electric shock. Tensile strength, covered above, explains why some materials are chosen for structural parts that get pulled or stretched.

Key Fact

Density, conductivity and tensile strength are physical and working properties used to justify material choice across every category in the exam.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Each material category has advanced materials beyond the core content — high carbon steel, tungsten steel and titanium for metals; packaging laminates for papers and boards; ABS, PET and PVC for polymers; microcontrollers for systems; viscose, acetate and Tencel for textiles; jelutong, larch and chipboard for timbers.
  • Density, conductivity and tensile strength are physical and working properties used to compare and justify material choices across every category.
  • Always link a named property to the specific use of a product when answering exam questions — this shows the reasoning examiners reward.

Analysing Products: The Ten Specification Criteria

Before you design anything for your own non-examined assessment (NEA), you need to know how to look critically at products that already exist. Analysing existing products teaches you what works, what does not, and how a designer balanced competing demands. The specification sets out ten criteria you must use whenever you analyse a product.

These criteria give your analysis structure, so it is not just a list of opinions. Every point you make should be linked to evidence from the product itself and to the needs of the people who will use it.

Key Fact

The ten criteria are: form, function, client and user requirements, performance requirements, materials and components/systems, scale of production and cost, sustainability, aesthetics, marketability, and consideration of innovation.

What Each Criterion Means

Form is the shape, look and structural arrangement of a product — for example, whether a kettle is rounded or angular. Function is what the product actually does and how well it performs that job. A well-designed product usually balances form and function so that it looks good and works well.

Client and user requirements are the needs, wants and preferences of the people who commissioned the product and the people who will use it every day. Performance requirements set out the technical standards a product must meet, such as how much weight it can hold or how long its battery lasts. Materials and components/systems describe what a product is made from and how its parts fit together to function as a whole.

Scale of production and cost consider whether a product is made as a one-off, in batches, or through mass production, and how this affects the cost of each unit. Sustainability looks at the environmental and social impact of the materials used, and how the product is disposed of at the end of its life.

Aesthetics covers the visual and sensory appeal of a product — its colour, texture and finish. Marketability asks whether the product will actually sell: does it appeal to its target market and stand out from competitors? Finally, consideration of innovation asks how original the product is compared with what already exists on the market.

Imagine analysing a modern kettle using all ten criteria. Form: a rounded body with a comfortable handle. Function: it boils water quickly and switches off automatically. Client and user requirements: an elderly user might need a lightweight kettle with a large, easy-to-read water gauge. Performance requirements: it should boil one litre of water within a set time. Materials: a stainless steel body with a heat-resistant polymer handle. Scale of production: it is mass produced, which keeps the unit cost low. Sustainability: the steel body is recyclable, but the polymer handle is harder to separate for recycling. Aesthetics: a brushed steel finish looks premium. Marketability: it is priced to compete with similar mid-range kettles. Innovation: a keep-warm function sets it apart from basic kettles on the shelf.

Learning from the Work of Past and Present Designers

The specification also requires you to investigate designers and companies, past and present, so you can see these ten criteria applied in the real world. Studying other people’s design decisions gives you a bank of ideas to draw on and helps you understand why certain solutions became popular with users.

Historical examples show how context shapes design. The nineteenth-century Arts and Crafts movement, associated with the designer William Morris, reacted against mass-produced Victorian goods by promoting hand-craftsmanship, natural materials and decorative pattern design — showing how social attitudes towards industrial production can drive a whole design movement.

More recent designers show how the same ten criteria apply to modern products. The German designer Dieter Rams, who worked for the electronics company Braun, became known for the idea that good products should be simple, functional and free of unnecessary decoration. Charles and Ray Eames became known for moulding plywood into curved shapes to make affordable, comfortable furniture. James Dyson is known for developing bagless cyclone vacuum cleaner technology, an example of consideration of innovation driving a whole company’s identity.

Key Fact

Studying past and present designers helps you generate a wider range of ideas and avoid design fixation — getting stuck on the first idea you think of instead of exploring genuine alternatives.

When you research a designer or company for your own notes, use the ten criteria as headings. For Dieter Rams and Braun, you could note: form and aesthetics — clean lines, minimal colour, geometric shapes; function — controls that are simple and intuitive; innovation — an approach that went on to influence product design at other companies, including Apple, decades later; marketability — a restrained style that helped Braun stand out from more decorative competitors of the time. Structuring your notes this way means you can reuse the same headings for any designer or company you study.

Using This Analysis in Your Own Project

In your NEA, this kind of product and designer analysis belongs in the investigate stage. It should feed directly into your design brief and specification, not sit as a separate, disconnected section. Remember that designing is iterative: you will return to analyse products and revisit designers’ ideas throughout your project, not just once at the start, as you test, evaluate and refine your own prototype.

When you write about a product or designer in an exam answer, use the ten criteria to organise your response. This shows the examiner that you understand the full range of factors shaping a design decision, rather than focusing on just one factor, such as aesthetics.

Design Contexts: Choosing the Right Material

Every specialist material category — metals, papers and boards, polymers, systems, textiles and timbers — asks the same underlying question: is this the right material for this product, in this context? When designing or modifying a product, you must apply your knowledge of materials, components and manufacturing processes to a specific design context. Section B of your exam tests this in depth for the material category you have specialised in, so you need to be able to justify material choices using solid reasoning, not just description.

Aesthetic Factors

Aesthetic factors shape how appealing a product is to its target market. Form, colour and texture apply across every material category — a brushed-steel toaster looks modern, while a warm oak table feels traditional. For papers and boards, surface graphics matter too, since packaging must catch a shopper’s eye on a crowded shelf. For textiles, lustre, sheen and shine become extra aesthetic considerations — a satin evening dress needs a very different fabric finish to a matte cotton t-shirt.

Key Fact

The three core aesthetic factors are form, colour and texture. Papers and boards add surface graphics; textiles add lustre, sheen and shine.

Environmental Factors

Every material has an ecological footprint. For metals, producing steel from raw ore uses large amounts of energy and can cause pollution, so recycled steel and aluminium are often preferred. For polymers, biodegradable options such as Biopol® break down naturally and reduce landfill waste. For timbers and textiles, upcycling — turning waste wood or fabric scraps into a new, higher-value product — cuts down on raw material demand. For systems, designers must follow the Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) Directive when selecting components, and the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Directive when planning disposal.

Corrosion and decay are ongoing environmental concerns for metals left untreated outdoors. Genetic engineering of fast-growing softwood species can reduce pressure on natural forests for timbers and some papers and boards. RoHS restricts substances such as lead in solder used inside electronic systems, while WEEE makes manufacturers responsible for the safe collection and recycling of electronic waste at end of life. Across every category, transportation, wastage and pollution during processing all add to a material’s total ecological footprint.

Availability Factors

Availability asks whether a material can be sourced reliably and affordably. Designers usually choose stock materials — standard sheets, bars or rolls kept ready by suppliers — because they are quick to obtain. Sometimes a product needs a specialist material instead, such as titanium for lightweight sports equipment or Kevlar for protective textiles. For metals, world market price also affects consumption and demand: when a metal becomes scarce, manufacturers may switch to an alternative. For polymers, availability is tied to global oil supply, since most polymers are made from crude oil. For systems, some components rely on scarce elements such as lithium and cobalt, which raises both availability and ethical concerns.

Cost Factors

Cost depends on the quality of material needed and the manufacturing processes required to shape it. For metals, the commodity price is set on the London Metal Exchange, so the cost of steel or aluminium can shift from month to month. Recycling also changes the cost picture: recycling steel or aluminium is often cheaper than processing virgin ore, because far less energy is needed. For polymers, cost tracks the world oil price. For textiles, transportation costs matter, since raw fibres such as cotton or wool are often shipped long distances before manufacture. For timbers, treatments such as fire-proofing or preservative tanalising add to the final cost.

Key Fact

Cost is driven by material quality, manufacturing processes needed, and market factors such as commodity price. Recycled metal is usually cheaper to process than virgin ore because it needs less energy.

Social Factors

Social factors cover how a material suits different groups of users, and how trends and fashion shift demand. A material that is popular with one age group or user group — brightly coloured acrylic for a teenager’s room accessory, for instance — may be entirely wrong for another. Fashion trends also move fast in textiles and papers and boards, meaning manufacturers must be ready to change materials and finishes as popularity shifts.

Cultural, Ethical Factors & Built-in Obsolescence

Cultural and ethical factors mean avoiding offence, making sure a material suits its intended market, and thinking about the wider effects of mass production. One recurring ethical issue is built-in obsolescence — designing a product so it wears out or becomes outdated sooner than it needs to, so customers buy again. This raises real ethical questions about waste and the consumer society, and it is a factor examiners expect you to weigh up when discussing material and product choices.

Fast-fashion textiles are sometimes criticised for encouraging built-in obsolescence — cheap synthetic fabrics that wear out quickly, driving repeat purchases. In systems, some manufacturers make batteries difficult to replace, forcing users to buy a whole new product rather than a component. Ethical designers instead consider repairability, using colour and language appropriately for the intended market, and avoiding offence to social or cultural groups when selecting decorative finishes or imagery.

Balancing the Factors: A Worked Example

Imagine designing a reusable water bottle. Stainless steel is durable, recyclable and looks premium, but it is heavier and its commodity price fluctuates. Polypropylene is cheap, lightweight and widely available as a stock material, but it has a poorer environmental reputation unless a recycled grade is specified. Neither material wins on every factor: the designer must prioritise according to the brief, the budget, and the target user — exactly the kind of reasoning an Evaluate question expects you to demonstrate.

Key Fact

No material scores highly on every selection factor. Strong answers show the trade-off — naming the factor that mattered most for a given product and context.

Applying This to Your Specialism

In Section B, you will apply these six factors — aesthetic, environmental, availability, cost, social, and cultural/ethical — to your chosen material category in depth. Practise naming a specific material, stating the relevant factor, and explaining exactly why that factor matters for the product in the question. That structure turns a vague description into a justified, marks-worthy answer.

Evaluating New & Emerging Technologies

Design and technology never stands still. New materials, smart components and manufacturing processes appear every year, and a designer must judge whether each one is actually worth using. This lesson explores how designers carry out critical evaluation of new and emerging technologies, and how ethical and environmental thinking shapes design decisions today and in the future. Getting this right matters for your exam — questions that ask you to ‘evaluate’ or ‘discuss’ are marked on the quality of your reasoning, not just on what you already know.

Criteria for Critical Evaluation

Before a new technology reaches a real product, designers ask practical questions first. Is there enough budget to buy, license or research the technology? Will it be ready within the project’s timescale, or is it still years away from reliable use? These two constraints alone can rule out a promising technology if a business cannot afford it or cannot afford to wait for it to mature. A dazzling material demonstrated in a lab is worthless to a company that needs a working product on shelves next year.

Three further questions matter just as much. Who is the product actually for — a child, an elderly user, or someone with a disability, and does the technology suit their needs? What materials does the technology require, and are they realistically available? Finally, does the business have the manufacturing capabilities needed to make the product reliably, in the quantities required? A brilliant idea that a factory cannot actually build, or cannot build accurately, is not yet a usable design solution.

Key Fact

Critical evaluation of a new technology weighs up budget constraints, timescale, who the product is for, the materials needed, and the manufacturing capabilities available before it reaches production.

Contemporary & Future Scenarios

Critical evaluation also means thinking beyond the immediate brief. A new technology can be judged against contemporary and future scenarios such as responses to natural disasters, medical advances, travel, global warming and communication. A low-cost, waterproof water filter might be evaluated for how well it could perform in a flood-relief effort. A new lightweight composite might be judged on whether it reduces fuel use in transport, helping to tackle global warming. A wearable sensor might be evaluated for its potential in medical advances, such as monitoring a patient’s heart rate remotely. Considering these scenarios helps a designer see whether a technology has a future beyond its first intended use.

A designer is evaluating a solar-powered charging unit. Against the criterion of natural disasters, it scores well — it needs no mains electricity, so it could recharge phones after a power cut. Against travel, it is useful for hikers with no access to sockets. Against communication, it keeps devices running when networks are needed most, such as during an emergency. Weighing these scenarios together helps the designer decide the charger is worth developing further, even though it costs more to make than a standard charger.

Ethical Perspectives

Ethical perspectives ask questions about people, not just performance. Where was the product actually made, and under what conditions were the workers employed? Who made it — was the workforce paid and treated fairly, or exploited to keep costs low? Who benefits most from the sale of the product — the manufacturer, the retailer, or the original producer of the raw material? Many companies now look for fair trade products when sourcing raw materials such as cotton or cocoa, so that producers in developing countries are not exploited by unfair pricing.

Key Fact

Ethical evaluation considers where a product was made, who made it, who benefits from it, and whether it meets fair trade standards.

Environmental Perspectives

Environmental perspectives focus on impact rather than people. Designers consider the use of materials — are they renewable, recycled, or scarce and finite? They also estimate a product’s carbon footprint, the greenhouse gases released in making, moving and using it.

Energy usage and consumption during manufacture and transportation both add to that footprint — shipping a product by air uses far more energy than moving the same product by sea. To bring all of this together into one clear picture, designers use life cycle analysis (LCA), tracking impact from raw material extraction right through to disposal or recycling.

LCA breaks a product’s environmental impact into four stages: extracting raw materials, manufacturing and processing, use by the consumer, and final disposal or recycling. A product that scores well at the manufacturing stage might still have a poor overall LCA if it cannot be recycled or safely disposed of at the end of its life, so every stage must be considered together.

Bringing It Together

No single factor decides whether a new technology should be used. A cheap, fast, ethically sourced material with a low carbon footprint might still fail if it cannot survive the stresses a product will face, or if a factory lacks the machinery to shape it accurately. Strong evaluation weighs practical, ethical and environmental perspectives against each other, and reaches a judgement supported by evidence — exactly what examiners reward when a question asks you to evaluate a technology rather than simply describe it.

From Initial Ideas to a Chosen Design

By this point in your non-examined assessment you will have generated a range of initial design ideas (NEA 2.1). The next three stages ask you to review those ideas, develop the strongest into a single chosen design, and then review that final choice before you start making. This is not a straight line through a checklist — the specification describes design as an iterative design process, meaning ideas are tested, evaluated and refined again and again as your project moves forward.

Reviewing Initial Ideas (NEA 2.2)

NEA stage 2.2 is worth 8 AO3 marks. You must analyse and evaluate how well each initial idea meets the design brief and the design specification. This means checking every idea against every relevant point in the specification, not simply deciding which idea you personally prefer. Ideas that meet the brief and specification are selected to take forward into development; ideas that only partly succeed are modified so they fit better, and ideas that cannot be made to work are dropped.

Key Fact

Reviewing initial ideas means: (1) analysing each idea against the specification, (2) deciding which ideas to take forward, and (3) modifying ideas that only partly meet the brief.

Developing the Chosen Design (NEA 2.3)

NEA stage 2.3 is the largest single stage in Design, worth 4 AO1 marks and 8 AO2 marks. You take the strongest idea, or ideas, forward from 2.2 and refine them into one chosen design. This includes carrying out further research if you need more information, and considering the design as a whole rather than looking at separate parts in isolation — a well-designed handle is no use if it does not fit the rest of the product. You should also incorporate feedback from any testing or modelling as you go, rather than saving it all for the final review.

A key skill here is modelling and simulation. You might test a mechanism with a card mock-up, check a fit using a 3D-printed part, or simulate a circuit before committing to it. Modelling lets you find problems while they are still cheap and quick to fix, rather than discovering them once the prototype is nearly finished.

NEA 2.3 requires calculations that determine material quantities and give technical detail clear enough that someone else could manufacture the product without asking you further questions.

For example, a polymer component in a chosen design measures 120 mm by 60 mm. Area of one component: $$120 \times 60 = 7200\text{ mm}^2$$ Converting to cm² by dividing by 100: $$7200 \div 100 = 72\text{ cm}^2$$ For a batch of 15 identical components: $$72 \times 15 = 1080\text{ cm}^2$$ of sheet polymer is needed, before allowing extra material for waste at the edges of the sheet.

Tolerances and Efficient Use of Material

Alongside material quantities, your technical detail should state a tolerance. No manufacturing process cuts a component to an exact size every single time, so a tolerance such as ±0.5 mm tells whoever makes the product how much variation is acceptable while the parts still fit and work together.

Calculations should also support efficient use of material. Marking out components close together on a sheet, or nesting shapes to leave minimal offcuts, reduces waste and cost. This links directly to the sustainability and cost factors you studied in the core content, and examiners expect you to apply that knowledge here, not just in Section A of the exam.

Key Fact

Calculation marks are earned through the correct formula, the correct steps shown as working, and the correct final answer. An unsupported final answer can lose method marks even when it happens to be right.

Reviewing the Chosen Design (NEA 2.5)

NEA stage 2.5 is worth 6 AO3 marks. Once you have a chosen design, you analyse the refinements you made and evaluate them with reference to feedback from others — your teacher, peers, or a client — not only your own opinion. You should also confirm that the materials, components and manufacturing techniques you have chosen are still appropriate now that the design is finalised.

Incorporating feedback well does not mean copying every suggestion you receive. It means weighing each piece of feedback against your specification and explaining why you accepted or rejected it. Explaining that reasoning is what separates a described change from a properly evaluated one.

These command words are not interchangeable. Describe asks for the main features of something, without reasons. Explain asks for reasons, so your answer needs a ‘because’. Evaluate asks you to weigh up strengths, weaknesses and alternatives and reach a supported judgement — a list of points with no judgement will not reach the top marks.

Why Investigation Comes First

Your design and make project — the non-exam assessment — begins with an Investigate stage before you design or make anything. You must show you understand a real design problem, find out what an end user actually needs, and turn that understanding into a written specification the rest of your project can be judged against. Skipping straight to sketching ideas without this groundwork loses marks, because examiners cannot see where your design decisions came from.

Identifying User Needs & the Design Problem

A contextual challenge sets a broad theme — for example, products for outdoor activities. Your first job is to identify the needs of the end user: the specific person or group who will use your prototype. From this you outline a design problem, a clear statement of what is going wrong or missing, and identify a need for a product that could solve it. A vague problem such as ‘people get cold outside’ is too broad — a stronger design problem names the user, the situation and the specific difficulty they face.

Key Fact

A design problem must name the end user, the situation they are in, and the specific difficulty they face. Vague problems lead to vague specifications and unfocused designs.

Researching Existing Products

Before generating your own ideas, you must investigate existing products that already try to solve similar problems, including work by past and present designers. Analysing an existing product means looking at its form, function, the materials and components used, how it is made, its cost, and how well it meets the client and user requirements. This tells you what already works, what could be improved, and gives you evidence to justify your own specification points.

A student investigating a design problem about carrying school equipment analyses an existing backpack. They note its form (the shape and size of the main compartment), its function (padded straps to spread the load), the materials used (nylon fabric, foam padding) and its approximate retail cost. They also note a weakness — the zip is not waterproof — which becomes evidence for a new specification point in their own project.

Research Strategies

Research should not stop at products. The specification also needs evidence from four other research strategies: market research into what potential users want, often shown as percentages or a graph of survey responses; research into the context in which the prototype will be used, such as where and when it will be carried; research into other possible materials that could be used instead of the obvious choice; and research into any sustainability issues connected to the intended prototype, such as how it could be disposed of or recycled. Each strategy should produce evidence you can point to later, not just a general impression.

Key Fact

The four required research strategies are: market research, research into the context of use, research into alternative materials, and research into sustainability issues.

Writing the Design Brief

Once you understand the problem and have gathered evidence, you write a design brief: a short statement that responds to the contextual challenge and addresses the needs and wants you identified. A design brief is not the same as a specification — it sets out the general aim of the project in a sentence or two, giving the reader a clear idea of what you intend to design and for whom.

Writing a Product Specification

The design brief is then expanded into a full product specification: a list of statements the finished prototype must meet. Each specification point should cover:

  • form — the shape, size and appearance of the product
  • function — what the product must do
  • user requirements — the needs of the end user identified in research
  • performance requirements — how well the product must work
  • materials and components — what it will be made from
  • scale of production — how many will be made
  • cost — the budget for materials and manufacture
  • sustainability — the environmental impact of materials and disposal

Every point in the specification must be technical, measurable and justified — not just a general aim. ‘The product should be lightweight’ is not measurable. ‘The product must weigh no more than 200 g so it can be carried comfortably by a child’ is technical, measurable and justified, because it gives a number and explains why that number matters, using evidence from your research.

These three command words are not interchangeable. Describe asks you to give an account of the main features of something, without needing reasons. Explain asks for a reason or set of reasons — you must say why something works, not just what it is. Evaluate asks you to weigh up strengths and weaknesses and reach a substantiated judgement; simply describing a product’s features when asked to evaluate it will not access the higher marks.

Setting Evaluation Criteria

The final part of writing a specification is identifying the criteria that will later be used to judge whether your prototype is successful. These criteria come directly from your specification points — if a point states the product must weigh no more than 200 g, then ‘the finished prototype weighs 200 g or less’ becomes a testable criterion you can check against at the Evaluate stage of your project.

Iterative, Not Linear

Investigation, designing, making and evaluating are described in the specification as a sequence, but in practice your project should follow an iterative design process: you test, evaluate and refine your ideas continually, returning to earlier stages when new evidence comes to light. A student might, for example, return to their specification and add a new point after testing a material sample shows it will not perform as expected.
